The bears are having their moment.

After predicting a top in the AI trade every month for the last 4 years, the bears finally got their moment last week.

However, in 3 to 6 months, we are going to look back at this correction and realize it was just that: a correction.

There is a widespread narrative right now that Nvidia, $NVDA, is quite literally going to collapse. This is a stock that was trading at a record high on October 6th, worth nearly $6 trillion, and the inventor of the most advanced chips in the world (it's not even close).

That's how deeply pessimistic sentiment has become over the last seven weeks.

Even if Nvidia produced half as much revenue as they are guiding for their next fiscal year, this company would still produce close to $400 billion in annual revenue.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 has posted three consecutive quarters with earnings growth above 25% and eight straight quarters of double-digit growth.

And, sentiment flipped so quickly that the S&P 500 closed the week 4.1 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average on Friday. Not even 2020 and 2008 saw such an occurrence.

The reality is that AI truly is the "next big thing" and the AI buildout is only accelerating.

Bears will sound smart, bulls will make money.

You got some things right and other things wrong, but in general, your overall construct is incorrect.  It is not the case that the other alts contributed all of their performance fees to their public companies, and that our shareholders don't benefit from the investment performance generated by our funds.  

It is true that Pershing Square Inc. ($PS) is structured differently from the other alternative asset managers (alts) like Blackstone, KKR, and others. Our unique structure is highly beneficial to our company and our shareholders, as I explain below.

In short, when Blackstone and the other alts went public, they contributed a substantial portion -- typically 40% to 60%, but not all of their incentive, performance, or promote compensation to the public company and retained the balance to compensate their employees.

The outcome of this approach has been suboptimal.  First, promote income, particularly from private equity funds, is highly volatile. It is only earned and paid when funds generate a return in excess of a preferred return and when a liquidity event happens, that is, when portfolio companies and/or the funds' real estate assets are sold. As a result, analysts and investors in the alts value the highly volatile income from incentive fees at a low multiple. 

Wall Street likes recurring and growing fee streams like management fees. It does not like volatile incentive fee income.

By contributing so much of their incentive fees to their public companies, the other alts did not retain enough incentive fees to pay their teams. The result is that the other alts grant large amounts of equity compensation to their employees in addition to the promote income they pay to their employees. This equity compensation dilutes reported earnings by as much as 20% or more.

In order to address these concerns, when we structured Pershing Square Inc. (PS) in anticipation of its public offering, we bifurcated the performance fee differently. Rather than giving Pershing Square Inc. a pro rata slice of our performance fees, we gave the public company a senior interest in our performance fee income -- what we call Preferred Performance Fees -- and employees retained a subordinate interest in the incentive fee income, what we call Subordinated Performance Fees. 

PS retains the performance fees on the first five percentage points of returns net of management fees from our funds that charge performance fees, and our employees receive the performance fees on returns above 5% if there are any.  

If our funds do not earn a return in excess of 5% in any year, any unpaid Preferred Performance Fees accrue into a future year or years until they are earned and paid.  In other words, the company and our shareholders get paid first before our employees.

As long as investors believe we can earn a gross compound return of 6.5% -- the 5% preferred return plus the 1.5% annual management fee -- over the long term (a high likelihood, in our view, in light of our investment strategy that has generated gross returns of nearly 20% for the last 23 years), Preferred Performance Fees are effectively economically equivalent to management fees and therefore deserving of a similar valuation multiple.

We believe our high-return investment strategy will allow us to not only earn the Preferred Performance Fees over time, but also enable us to continually earn Subordinate Performance Fees that we can use to compensate, recruit and retain high quality talent. As a result, we don't need to issue large amounts of stock and option compensation to employees like the other alternative investment managers, minimizing the risk of dilution to shareholders.

[PS also benefits from the fact that, as is typical in the hedge fund industry, we earn incentive fees from both realized and unrealized gains so we are not forced to sell assets in order to generate returns. It’s not good to be $NVDA and on the short list of companies that Congress investigated for illegal activities. In most cases they already secretly knew crimes were committed. Go figure. We’ll do Enron for fun, but this was right after bankruptcy.

(1) Congress publicly alleged illegal activity before criminal convictions

In January 2002, Representative Billy Tauzin, chairman of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, announced that congressional investigators had uncovered:

“substantial evidence of illegal activity”

He specifically identified transactions involving Enron’s partnerships and its auditor, Arthur Andersen.

This was a congressional allegation based on investigative evidence, not a criminal conviction. 

(2) Congress uncovered how Enron concealed debt

The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations examined more than one million pages of subpoenaed documents.

Its July 8, 2002 report concluded that Enron’s board knowingly permitted billions of dollars in off-the-books activity.

The committee found that these arrangements made Enron’s financial condition appear stronger than it actually was.

Congress also documented conflicts involving CFO Andrew Fastow and his private investment partnerships. 

Primary congressional report:

The Role of the Board of Directors in Enron's Collapse — July 2002⁠

(3) Congress exposed the banks’ involvement

This is particularly relevant to modern corporate financing.

On July 23, 2002, the Senate began hearings examining how major financial institutions helped Enron structure transactions that affected its reported financial statements.

The investigations examined financing arrangements that could make borrowing resemble operating transactions.

These included transactions involving major banks such as Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase.

The central concern was whether Enron had effectively disguised debt and manipulated its reported cash flow. 

Primary source:

Senate announcement: Banks' complicity in Enron's collapse⁠

(4) Congress established failures by financial regulators

In October 2002, the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee released findings concerning the SEC, credit rating agencies and Wall Street analysts.

The investigation concluded that multiple layers of financial oversight had failed to identify or adequately address Enron’s problems.

That finding was particularly important because Enron had maintained access to financing despite its deteriorating financial condition. 

(5) Did Congress uncover the fraud before prosecutors proved it?

Yes.

Congress publicly documented significant evidence of wrongdoing before the major criminal trials concluded.

Its investigations helped establish how the fraud worked, while the DOJ and FBI pursued criminal accountability.

The FBI describes the Enron investigation as one of the most complex white-collar investigations in its history.

My Editorial In Barrons Over The Weekend

I authored an editorial  - What  A Corporate Scandal Says About Our Bull Market - in this weekend's "Other Voices" section of Barrons magazine. I hope you enjoy reading it. 

COMMENTARY  

What a Corporate Scandal Says About Our Bull Market  
By Doug Kass  
Nov 20, 2026 12:06 pm EST

Scandals like Nvidia’s inevitably emerge as markets peak.   

It always happens at the end of an economic expansion, as a bull market begins to wind  down: The risks, the frauds, and the corrupt suddenly appear in broad daylight.  

Sometimes they come in the form of overexuberant corporate executives who have been quietly skating on the thin ice of business ethics, like former Nvidia     CEO Jensen Huang. 

Or they emerge from within our country’s leadership, when figures like  former plumber, now Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and former reality TV  star, now Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, are exposed as incompetent lackeys. 

But the truth  always surfaces when the tides go out.  Major scandals featuring questionable figures—Enron, WorldCom, Tyco, Countrywide  Credit, Joe Granville, the savings and loan crisis—all appeared late in their respective  economic and market cycles.  

Seen in this light, the recent revelation of the Nvidia CEO’s affairs with an executive at the  firm and an alleged Chinese spy, and his company’s sales to the latter’s Singapore-based  shell company, which potentially routed banned Nvidia chips to China, is a classic late-cycle  phenomenon. (The Washington Post has also reported that President Donald Trump’s  stake in Nvidia had risen as high as $62 million this year, raising more questions about  impropriety).  

Huang is far from the first business leader to fall from grace in such terrible fashion —the  predicament of being human never changes.  

Collectively, we tend toward excess. In July 2007, as some of Bear Stearns’ hedge funds  were collapsing and New Century Financial was deep in bankruptcy proceedings, Chuck  Prince, then Citigroup CEO, told the Financial Times that “as long as the music is playing,  you’ve got to get up and dance. We’re still dancing.”  Bankers and investors danced over cracks in the credit and housing markets that appeared  in the winter of 2007, just as they did in late 1999 as the dot-com boom neared maturation.  

Time and time again, market participants have shown they will dance right up until the  music stops. They are confident or haughty enough to think that they can anticipate the  signposts of a market top. Of course, assessing when an excess is reaching a tipping point is  never so easy. 

But such a moment is guaranteed: Excesses are never permanent.  

In hindsight, former Federal Reserve Chair Alan Greenspan’s “irrational exuberance” idea  wasn’t wrong, just premature. Irrationality, hubris, and complacency are all signposts of  expiring bull markets. Investors lower their guard. Corporate accounting guardrails drop,  as erroneous claims like “price is truth” and questionable accounting practices like “non GAAP” earnings per share gain acceptance. 

Large market drawdowns follow. 

I believe we are nearing a similar decline, but there are differences compared with 1999  and 2007 that make today’s market shakiness more troubling.  The magnitude of investment in AI is much larger than that in the internet at the height of  the dot-com boom. 

Hyperscalers’ capital expenditures as a share of gross domestic product  this year is more than double the telecoms’ capex in 1999, according to Apollo Global  Management. The federal government is also far more significantly leveraged than it was in  2007—the debt as a share of GDP is roughly twice as high now.  

Another difference today is the leverage in the cryptocurrency and private-equity markets.  New risks accompany a more-levered market structure, in which passive investing  activities like quant strategies and electronic-traded funds that “worship at the altar of

posts.text:
Korean media report that Samsung plans to add a production line capable of processing 20,000 wafers per month at its X2 NAND flash fab in Xi’an, China, bringing the fab to its full production capacity.

X2 currently produces 100,000 V6 NAND wafers and 10,000 V9 NAND wafers per month. The fab can handle up to 130,000 wafers per month.

Samsung plans to dedicate the new line entirely to V9 and convert 20–30% of its existing V6 capacity to V9 production. The expansion and conversion would raise X2’s V9 capacity to 50,000–60,000 wafers per month.

Samsung plans to build an electroplating line in unused cleanroom space at X2, with equipment move-in expected around February 2027. The company plans to send engineers from its South Korean operations to Xi’an with the aim of completing the expansion by November 2027.

posts.text:
AMD’nin 2028 hedefi yaklaşık 794 dolar, Nvidia’nınki ise 457 dolar. Yani AMD’nin hisse fiyatı daha yüksek görünüyor ama asıl büyük potansiyel Nvidia’da olabilir. Yanlış okumadınız.

▬ AMD: 2028’de yaklaşık 794 dolar hedefi, mevcut seviyeye göre yaklaşık %45 yukarı.

▬ Nvidia: 2028 hedefi yaklaşık 457 dolar bu, fiyatın kabaca üçe katlanması anlamına geliyor.

Peki nasıl?

AMD’nin hikayesi daha pay alarak büyüme hikayesi. Şirket sunucu işlemcilerinde pazar payını artırıyor. Üçüncü çeyrekte sunucu işlemci pazarındaki payı yıllık bazda 7,7 puan artarak %35,5’e çıkmış. Bu, Intel’in yıllardır oturduğu masada yeni sandalye açmak demek.

Ayrıca AMD, 2027’de sunucu gelirinin ikiye katlanmasından bahsediyor. Tabii bunun arkasında tek bir ürün değil, veri merkezi talebi, yapay zeka altyapısı ve yeni nesil işlemciler var. Yani AMD’nin işi sadece Nvidia’ya rakip olmak değil; Intel’in klasik sunucu alanında da yer kapmak.

Nvidia’nın durumu ise bambaşka.

Şirket bu yıl hisse tarafında zorlanmış olabilir ama iş sonuçları hala çok güçlü. Son çeyrekte gelir yıllık %103 artarak 115,8 milyar dolara çıkmış. Kârlılık da benzer hızda büyümüş. Normalde insan böyle büyüme sonrası fiyatın da aynı hızda gitmesini bekler ama piyasalar gelecekte bu hız sürer mi? sorusunu sürekli soruyor.

Aslında asıl mesele bu.

Nvidia çok büyüdüğü için yatırımcı artık sadece büyümeye değil, büyümenin sürdürülebilirliğine bakıyor. Makaledeki senaryoda Nvidia’nın 2029 mali yılında hisse başına kârının 21,75 dolara ulaşması ve değerleme çarpanının 21 kat seviyesine inmesi bekleniyor. Yani şirket büyürken, yatırımcının ödediği “büyüme primi” biraz normalleşebilir.

Bu yüzden Nvidia’nın fiyatı üçe katlansa bile, değerleme çarpanı düşebilir. AMD’de ise tablo ters: büyüme daha ılımlı ama pazar payı ve kâr artışı değerlemeyi taşıyabilir.

Mesela şöyle düşünün.

AMD: Pazarda daha fazla yer alıyorum, karım hızla artıyor.

Nvidia: Zaten devasa yer alıyorum, şimdi bu devasa büyümeyi ne kadar sürdürebilirim?

İkisi de yapay zeka altyapısının kazananı. Ama riskleri farklı.

AMD için risk, Nvidia’nın ekosistem gücünü kırmanın ne kadar zor olduğu. Nvidia için risk ise müşterilerin harcama temposu, rekabet ve çok yüksek beklentilerin fiyatına yansımış olması.

Çok büyük olmak her zaman çözüm getirmiyor. Bazen en büyük sorun, herkesin sizden çok şey beklemesidir.

Bu yüzden AMD hikâyesi “yakalayan şirket”, Nvidia hikâyesi ise “liderliğini koruyan şirket” hikâyesi. 2028’e kadar ikisinin de yolu uzun.

#AMD #Nvidia

posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text:
After a brutal week in the market, it is easy to believe that things can only get worse. But history offers a different perspective.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has experienced 81 comparable sessions with losses of at least 3.5% for which forward-return data is available. Historically, the median return following those sessions was +1.80% after one month, +6.44% after three months, and +21.73% after one year. The index finished higher in 64.2% of cases after one month, 74.1% after three months, and 82.7% after one year.

That doesn’t mean the bottom is in. Some of the biggest rebounds in history happened during bear markets, only to be followed by another leg lower. A sharp bounce can mark the beginning of a recovery, or simply provide temporary relief before more pain. The difference is what happens afterward.

Right now, I am watching market breadth, volatility, yields, and whether earnings expectations remain intact. Another retest of the lows would not surprise me. Markets rarely move in a straight line from panic to recovery.

But one terrible week, one brutal selloff, or even a period of extreme fear does not determine the next 12 months. Historically, the longer the investment horizon, the more recovery has favored patient investors.

Don’t confuse uncertainty with the absence of opportunity. Protect your capital, keep some cash, avoid emotional decisions, and let the market show you when conditions are improving.

Fear is loudest when prices are falling. Opportunity usually requires patience before it becomes obvious.

Not financial advice.

posts.text: I would push your argument a bit further — it is even possible that the true underlying inflation is closer to Fed’s target than data show. The rapid advancement of AI (as well as other advancements like GLP1) has introduced several measurement problems in CPI / PCE that likely inflated the measure.  Back in the 90s the Boskin Commission had found that CPI was inflated by roughly 1.0 ppt due to the tech boom. The politicized environment today render the Fed unwilling or unable to consider these nuances. The said thing is, this current “last hard mile” of inflation could well be a costly statistical error.

The quiet days tell you the most. Nov 17 and Nov 19 were both down days with dispersion near the median. That isn't stocks splitting apart. That's everything getting sold together.

EXTREME (95th+ pct) · 343 days
SPY avg 20d: +1.08% · avg 60d: +3.97%
QQQ avg 60d: +8.50%

That average hides what matters most: how long the stretch lasts. Isolated 1 to 2 day EXTREME spikes averaged +12.2% for SPY over the next 60 days. Stretches that ran 30+ days, GFC and COVID, averaged -20.4%.

TWENTY-FOUR HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 7PM TO 7PM on 11/22/26

The channel prong widened on every side in this window. The Wall Street Journal named the operator behind Megaspeed and a successor venture still taking in Nvidia hardware, the New York Times put a named ministry and minister behind China's chip procurement campaign, the Director of National Intelligence confirmed on the record that Alice Huang and Megaspeed are under investigation, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, asked directly, refused to rule out Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO.

THE MAN BEHIND MEGASPEED

• The Wall Street Journal (Stu Woo, November 21, 2026) identifies Li Ming, a 52-year-old Chinese national, as a central operator behind Megaspeed alongside Alice Huang. Per the Journal's reporting, Singapore prosecutors allege Li bought computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips and lied to the American supplier, claiming the hardware was for his local company, Luxuriate Your Life; the servers were instead shipped to neighboring Malaysia and then to an unnamed third location.
• Per the same reporting, Li had been working with Alice Huang and her husband Kang Wei for years by the time Singapore filed fraud charges in February 2025. The three set up a chain of partners in Southeast Asia to funnel advanced computing power to Chinese customers, acquired the Singaporean unit of a Chinese video game company and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang registered as a company director.
• Megaspeed brought servers to Malaysia and provided legal offshore computing power to Alibaba. In violation of U.S. export controls, per the Journal, some of those servers were sent to a Shanghai tech company called Century Litong.
• The Journal reports Megaspeed largely went dark in Singapore after Alice Huang's departure, and the team behind it is now running a new venture, Novagate Cloud, set up in 2025. Novagate says on its website it is an Nvidia cloud partner operating at least two data centers with Nvidia's leading-edge Blackwell chips. In the first five months of 2026, per the Journal, Novagate received at least $300 million worth of hardware containing Nvidia chips at one of its entities in Malaysia. That figure is the Journal's own figure for that venture and window.
• Concordant carriages of the same reporting add that Li is out on bail, that Nvidia put Megaspeed on an internal no-sell list in June 2025, and that Megaspeed says its business is lawful. The Journal original is paywalled; the reporting above rests on the Journal's investigation as quoted and summarized in the window.

BEIJING'S CHIP CAMPAIGN

• The New York Times reported on November 21, 2026 that China's Ministry of State Security has run a covert campaign for at least two years to circumvent U.S. semiconductor export controls and secure advanced AI chips. Per the Times, Minister of State Security Chen Yixin is leading the effort and has assembled a working group that reports directly to him, whose mission includes helping Chinese companies obtain and smuggle advanced chips and gathering intelligence on the global semiconductor supply chain.
• The Times reporting rests on current and former intelligence officials in Asia, the United States and Europe, as carried in multiple concordant summaries of the piece. The same summaries record the Times' limiting fact: it has not been confirmed what specific role Alice Huang played in the Ministry's chip procurement operation, and China has denied the espionage allegations as groundless. The Times original is paywalled and was not read firsthand.

Then the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act of 1989 gave the central bank one job, price stability, and required it to agree on a numeric target with the government.

posts.text:
The 2% inflation target was randomly set by a dude in New Zealand decades ago… based on his gut! 

Grok says: It started with an off-the-cuff remark from New Zealand's Finance Minister, Roger Douglas, and central bank staff then turned it into an official number.

In April 1988, New Zealand's inflation had been running in double digits. When Douglas was asked on TV what he was aiming for, he said something like "around 0 or 1 percent." That wasn't based on any model. 

He basically blurted it out, and the Reserve Bank's officials have since said they were caught off guard.

Then the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act of 1989 gave the central bank one job, price stability, and required it to agree on a numeric target with the government. 

The first agreement, signed in March 1990 by Governor Don Brash and Finance Minister David Caygill, set a range of 0 to 2% to be hit by 1992. Staff justified the range after the fact. 

They argued that measured inflation probably overstates real inflation by about a percentage point, because price indexes miss quality improvements. They also wanted some room above zero so the economy wouldn't slip into deflation.

From there, the number spread around the world. Canada adopted a target in 1991, the UK in 1992, and others followed. Countries settled on about 2% as the midpoint, and the Fed made 2% official in January 2012 under Ben Bernanke. 

Later academic work defended 2% for reasons like leaving room to cut interest rates. But the number's origin really does trace back to a politician's TV answer, not to research.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
That still gets the cause backward. The construction and zoning reform are what bring rents down. Rent control doesn't add to that, it works against it. Stanford's San Francisco study found rent control cut rental supply by 15% and pushed citywide rents up about 5%. The biggest meta-analysis, covering nearly 200 studies, found it reduces new construction. So pairing it with a building push means one policy fighting the other.

The defensible version is narrower. Light rent stabilization that exempts new construction can protect existing tenants without doing much damage. But if a city is building aggressively and reforming zoning, that's what's doing the work. Rent control is along for the ride at best and a drag at worst.

posts.text: Set aside the stock market, the real indicator telling us the AI bubble has popped is in the bond market

quoted.text:
Most investors are watching tech stocks while missing what's happening in the AI credit markets:

HSBC reportedly sold $300 million in data centre loans at roughly 85 cents on the dollar, a 15% haircut. ING tried unloading another $500 million but couldn't attract sufficient bids at acceptable prices. Now it's negotiating individual sales.

Reuters is also reporting that banks are becoming reluctant to finance additional AI projects, even those backed by major technology companies.

The timing couldn't be worse. Goldman Sachs estimates hyperscaler debt issuance will surge 68%, from $250 billion in 2026 to $420 billion in 2027, precisely when lenders are becoming more cautious.

I've seen this movie before. As I discuss in my book, the shale oil boom and Canadian cannabis were both built on enormous expectations for future growth and the assumption that capital would remain readily available. I watched both industries discover what happens when those expectations collide with a mismatch in expectations vs what was actually delivered.

AI may very well transform the world, just as shale transformed American energy production. But that doesn't mean every dollar invested will earn an adequate return. When an investment boom depends on an endless supply of capital, the biggest risk isn't whether Jensen Huang comes back. It's whether the lenders do.

posts.name: Ben Woodward, CFA
posts.text:
The "dip buyers will save us" narrative rests on a small sample of mild VIX spikes while ignoring the fat-tail events that define real crises. Here are the salient counterpoints:
 
1. The 1987 and 2008 tails dwarf anything in your small sample.
The VIX precursor hit a closing high of 150.19 on Black Monday 1987, with intraday levels even higher . During the GFC, the VIX closed at 89.53 in October 2008 . Your sample's threshold of "at least 16.5 points" barely scratches the surface of what true panic looks like. A 35.9 VIX is elevated—not existential.‌￼‌￼‌￼
 
2. Even moderate VIX spikes have preceded further pain, not just relief.
The S&P 500 has always experienced further drawdowns in the 12 months following VIX spike events, averaging a 9.9% pullback ranging from 1.5% to 24% . The relief rally after the first spike does not immunize you from the second leg down.‌￼‌￼
 
3. The "100% hit rate" claim is survivorship bias in miniature.
A few occurrences since 1990 is not a statistical foundation. The 1990 event (oil shock/recession) and 2008 (systemic banking collapse) both saw VIX spikes followed by weeks of additional selling before any durable bottom.‌￼
 
4. VIX spikes signal capitulation—but timing the bottom is a different game.
Extreme VIX readings do tend to precede positive 12-month forward returns . But the path matters: a risk-adjusted approach that reduced exposure during high-VIX regimes produced a higher Sharpe ratio (0.54) than buying the dip above VIX 30 (0.47) . The signal is real; but the trade is not free.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Buy when the VIX spikes, not when the headlines clear

A sharp rise in the VIX has repeatedly been followed by solid equity returns. The pattern is clear enough that it is worth revisiting after the latest episode.

On 20 November the VIX jumped 9.29 points to 37.73. The S&P 500 fell 3.43 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 5.95 per cent. Since the start of 1996 there have been 90 sessions in which the VIX rose by more than five points in a single day. 

In the periods that followed those days, the median forward return for the S&P 500 was 5.62 per cent over three months, 10.86 per cent over six months and 19.87 per cent over one year. The Nasdaq 100 recorded corresponding median gains of 8.40 per cent, 16.66 per cent and 31.14 per cent. Returns are measured from the close on the day of the spike.

The current volatility term structure reinforces the contrary signal. Spot VIX is above the levels priced three and six months ahead, indicating that investors are paying a premium for near-term protection. Fear is concentrated in the present.

A violent sell-off changes quoted prices immediately. It does not erase the customers, competitive positions or cash-generation capacity of sound businesses. The practical implication is selective: quality and diversified equity exposure have historically been the assets that recovered most reliably once the immediate panic subsided.

Markets rarely present attractive entry points under calm headlines. The more common setting is falling prices and elevated demand for protection. The historical record after large daily VIX increases shows that those moments have, on average, rewarded investors who were prepared to act while others were still focused on the risks that had already materialised.

quoted.text:
Everyone is scratching his head after the recent market sell-off, but it’s really not that complicated. It’s pure math. Let’s take a look, shall we?

At their peaks, the major listed AI-exposed companies (Mag7 plus key chip, foundry, and infrastructure names) were worth roughly $28–32 trillion. Add Anthropic’s post-IPO valuation of about $1.2–1.5 trillion and an expected OpenAI post-IPO figure around $1.5 trillion, and the total sits in the $30–35 trillion range, approaching half the entire US equity market (recently ~$70–72 trillion).

Once a single theme absorbed that much capital, further large gains required either massive new inflows or more money pulled from everything else. At some point neither was available at the necessary scale. Expecting these names to double again from those peaks implied an incremental $30+ trillion of market value. The rest of the US market was only ~$40 trillion; global equity markets, bonds, and private capital held no unused liquidity of that magnitude ready for AI multiples. Leverage, retail flows, and foreign capital were already heavily committed.

The arithmetic simply stopped working. Prices could no longer be justified by any realistic path of further capital absorption. The pullback was the delayed recognition that the liquidity sucked into the trade had nowhere left to come from. It’s really that simple. Seriously, what were people thinking buying these names at multi-trillion valuations? That they would double again in three months?

posts.text:
This is not buy the dip. Just that part will get you killed during a fundamentally driven bear market which this could be.  This is a two part strategy that I try to employ to avoid massive losses and hopefully make money even when in a bear market.  

What I try to do is sell when fundamentals might be turning against you (in this case data centers getting pushed out in early October.) 

As of this Friday (11/20) it is now buy and overweight technically oversold conditions that give you great odds of a rally. 

But the next thing that many investors forget, which is easy to do when stocks are going straight up, will be to sell this back down to market weight or underweight when the odds are not in your favor again and their is a fundamental reason to be more circumspect. 

This is the part that is arguably harder to figure out- when to cut back. Stocks can mathematically go up infinitely as we saw during the meme stock craze. Investors tend to worry the least when they are making money versus when they are losing which is backwards.  

Best of luck and Happy Thanksgiving.

posts.text: Elon is deep in the details

quoted.text:
In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

Q @carlquintanilla  Speaking of your tweet on the short selling stoppage imposed outside of the US this weekend: 

Here is a Financial Times editorial I wrote years ago in the middle of The Great Recession in 2008:

This Blame Game Is Short On Logic

By Douglas Kass  AUG 21 2008

After acquiring General Re in 1998, Warren Buffett, the veteran investor, learnt the hard way that “derivatives are like hell, easy to enter but almost impossible to exit”.

Four years later, Mr Buffett, chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, argued that highly complex financial instruments and derivatives were time bombs and that these “financial weapons of mass destruction” might harm the econ­omic system. His caution was prescient – like that of many others who have identified company frauds or diagnosed previous credit cycles gone wild.

Yet most of these gloomy messengers have been ignored.

Since Mr Buffett’s warning, financial markets have imploded and policymakers have failed to address the abuses that created the crisis, from the excess leverage of banks to ratings agency failures. Instead, public policy has become focused on a blame game aimed at res­tricting the short-selling of securities – especially of a financial kind.

In July, Christopher Cox, chairman of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, announced a plan to curb improper (naked) short-selling. In doing so he has (de facto) attempted to limit the activity of short-sellers. Mr Cox seems to be implicitly blaming the shorts for the unprecedented fall of bank, ­government-sponsored agency and brokerage stocks over the past year – even though short-sellers were the very group that warned of the dangerous credit cycle and its consequences.

Short-selling runs deep in financial history. Perhaps the first case dates to 1609 when the Dutch trader, Isaac Le Maire, targeted the shares of the shipping company Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie (the Dutch East India Company). VOC was the first multinational corporation in history and had broad powers. Nonetheless, Le Maire, concerned about threats of attack by English ships, sold VOC’s shares short. After learning about Le Maire’s tactics, the stock exchange governing VOC’s trading banned short-selling (although the ban was later revoked). In the early 1630s, the Dutch economy fell into a depression following a speculative peak in the trading of tulips.

Again, short-selling raised the ire of regulators, many of whom saw it as magnifying the effect on the Dutch economic downturn. As a result, England banned short-selling outright. Almost 420 years later – in the late 1920s – short-sellers warned of the consequences of speculation. But in the aftermath of the Wall Street crash of 1929, many blamed them and the uptick rule – which banned short-selling on downticks – was instituted (and stayed in effect until 2007).

More regulation governing short-selling came into force in 1940, with a ban on mutual funds from short-selling (though that law was lifted in 1997). In early 2005, the SEC again sought to restrict the practice. Yet short-sellers have served as financial watchdogs, as many of their warnings have been spot on. The delusional dotcom boom in the late 1990s brought Cassandra-like utterings from the short-selling cabal that proved insightful but were largely ignored.

After the subsequent 75 per cent collapse of the Nasdaq, a bull market in corporate fraud emerged and short-sellers such as David Rocker, founder of Rocker Partners, highlighted accounting problems at companies such as Sunbeam, Tyco and Lernout & Hauspie. Kynikos’ Jim Chanos played a role in uncovering the largest fraud in history when his contrary-minded analysis warned of Enron’s accounting shenanigans – which were emulated (but ignored by investors) in the banks’ recent dalliance with structured investment vehicles.

In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

posts.name: jeroen blokland
posts.text:
A 3% primary surplus for 30 years?

Outgoing French President Macron has floated the idea (again) of writing budget discipline into the constitution.

It may sound promising, at least for French government bond spreads. In reality, enforcing such discipline would likely provoke enormous social and political unrest.

To prevent debt from rising further from its current 120% of GDP, France would need a primary surplus of roughly 1%. To bring debt down to the 60% threshold enshrined in the Maastricht Treaty, it would need a primary surplus of at least 3% of GDP. And even then, it would take 30 years of that surplus to reach the 60% threshold.

And that is before taking into account interest expenses, which are projected to rise by 2,5% of GDP in the next 10 years. Without offsetting measures, that means even larger deficits. For 2027 and 2028, France is already expected to run deficits well above 5% of GDP.

In addition, France has one of the world's most expensive welfare systems, with social spending exceeding 30% of GDP. As the French population ages, that share will only grow. Add defense, energy, healthcare, and everything needed to restore competitiveness and growth, and the pressure on public finances is enormous. Deficits approaching 10% of GDP are far more realistic than a balanced budget, let alone a surplus.

Achieving a sustained primary surplus would require a combination of significantly higher taxes, already among the highest in the world, and deep cuts to public spending. That means confronting the welfare state, including politically explosive measures such as raising the retirement age to something like 70. After what we have seen in recent months, the French are unlikely to simply accept that. The social and political consequences would be devastating.

Macron's constitutional budget rule, Mélenchon's call to cancel French debt held by the ECB, and Le Pen's promise to return debt to 60% of GDP are all aimed at one thing: lowering interest expenses.

None resolves the fundamental conflict between fiscal sustainability and political reality. The economic and political consequences of implementing these proposals would be enormous.

Which brings us back to the “easiest” route heavily indebted governments have repeatedly taken: artificially low interest rates and higher inflation.
For politicians, that is a much easier path to sustaining the debt burden.

For savers and bondholders, it is another story.

As noted earlier, Trump's tariff threat created an arbitrage opportunity in copper, sending prices soaring as it pulled an enormous amount of metal into US warehouses before the duties could take effect.

That left the rest of the world, and China in particular, short of supply.

On top of that came a flood of financial capital, drawn to copper as a key input for AI infrastructure.

Bloomberg now reports that the copper scarcity narrative has lost steam since the US midterms, as the tariffs never arrived and, following the latest electoral rebuke of Trump (which weakened figures such as Lutnick), even the biggest bulls see new levies as less likely.

So it seems that the base case has shifted away, leaving a decidedly bearish outlook.

The market is now weighing what happens if the "sea" of copper piled up in the US flows back out: the global market would be comfortably supplied, and the scarcity that had been propping up prices would disappear.

The recent selloff in AI stocks and shifting expectations for further interest-rate hikes have also added another layer of pressure on industrial metals.

#Copper

posts.text:
While algos and hedge fund factor baskets have been pitching uranium shares in pure capitulation, the spot uranium price is holding firm amidst an active mid and long-term market. 

This present liquidity event has been sufficient to force certain financial players to sell some of their uranium holdings over the past couple of weeks. That selling has been met with ample buying interest, resulting in essentially zero downward pressure on the spot price. 

There is significant mid-term utility demand, currently, to support some carry trades getting done at current prices. Reading between the lines — $90 spot + cost of carry + cost of capital + profit = mid-term base escalated likely getting done ~$110/lb. (roughly). 

Last week, KHNP issued a uranium tender for just over 13m lbs. delivered over a ten-year period. With 26 reactors at 15-year high capacity factors and 4 more reactors being built, KHNP’s 10-12M+ lb. annual burn rate and layered buying make another tender likely within 12 months.

This is in addition to more contracting from India soon to be announced, Russia buying across the fuel cycle, and timeline extension announcements for important supply development projects are inevitable. 

I can’t tell you if the past week was the equities’ bottom. But I can tell you that this correlated selling has nothing to do with the fundamentals, and that this story is FAR from over.

posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text:
THE CHRISTMAS SETUP: WHEN FEAR CREATES OPPORTUNITY 🎄

This is one of my favourite times of the year, and for once, several pieces may be starting to line up. Yields are cooling, oil is pulling back, the Fed decision is approaching, and speculative growth stocks have been hit hard. Some of the names I have been tracking are down 20–40% in a single week. This is not a reason to blindly buy everything, but when sentiment becomes extreme and prices reset this aggressively, it is time to start paying attention.

The Santa Claus rally historically covers the final five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January. Historically, that period has been positive roughly 76% of the time, with an average return of around 1.25%. But seasonality is not a guarantee. The edge has weakened in recent years, and markets have reminded us that macro conditions, positioning, liquidity, and sentiment matter far more than the calendar. I am not betting on Christmas. I am watching for a potential window where several conditions begin working in our favour.

The macro picture is becoming interesting. Treasury yields have pulled back meaningfully, easing some of the pressure on growth stocks and companies whose valuations depend heavily on future cash flows. Oil has also cooled, potentially helping inflation expectations. The market is approaching another important Fed decision, and much of the expected move appears priced in. What matters now is whether yields continue lower, inflation stabilizes, and the Fed avoids delivering a surprise that forces markets to reprice risk all over again.

Small caps and speculative growth stocks have been among the hardest hit during this selloff. These are the companies most sensitive to tightening financial conditions, rising yields, liquidity, and investor appetite for risk. When fear takes over, investors often sell first and ask questions later. That creates indiscriminate selling, where fundamentally different businesses can get caught in the same wave. Eventually, the market begins separating companies with real progress, improving fundamentals, sufficient liquidity, and credible execution from those simply surviving on a future promise.

That is where opportunity and risk coexist. A stock falling 30% does not automatically make it cheap. A company can be down another 30% from here. Some businesses will recover, some will need more capital, and some may never regain their previous highs. The objective is not to chase the biggest losers. It is to identify where selling pressure begins to exhaust itself, where price stabilizes, and where risk-to-reward becomes attractive enough to justify a position.

Tax-loss selling, portfolio rebalancing, year-end positioning, and reduced liquidity can create additional volatility into December. But once forced selling fades, sentiment shifts, and money begins looking for beaten-down opportunities again, the same stocks that felt impossible to own during the selloff can move quickly. We do not need to predict the exact bottom. We need to recognize when the conditions are changing.

I am not calling for an immediate V-shaped recovery, nor am I suggesting the market has already bottomed. This is still a fragile environment, and another leg down remains possible. But after a significant reset, the best opportunities often begin forming when most investors are exhausted, pessimistic, and no longer interested in looking at their portfolios.

I am watching yields, oil, inflation, the Fed, market breadth, and price action closely. If conditions improve, I want to be prepared, not chasing the rally after it has already happened. If conditions deteriorate further, cash gives us the flexibility to wait. The market does not reward impatience. Sometimes the best trade is doing nothing. Sometimes the best opportunity appears when everything looks uncomfortable.

posts.text:
🚨 HERE IS THE ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION FOR THIS SELLOFF THAT ALMOST NO ONE IS DISCUSSING.

The market may not simply be liquidating crowded trades.

It may be front-running a 2027 free-cash-flow margin squeeze.

We tested 77 S&P 100 companies across roughly 14 years of quarterly data.

The result was clear:

Long-term interest rates were not the cash-flow killer. 

Inflation was.

For every one-percentage-point increase in core CPI, company free-cash-flow margins fell roughly 0.5 percentage points two to four quarters later.

Core CPI:
-FCF margin impact: approximately -0.5 percentage points
-Peak lag: two quarters
-t-stat: -4.4

Core PCE:
-FCF margin impact: approximately -0.6 percentage points
-Peak lag: three quarters
-t-stat: -3.3

Headline CPI:
-FCF margin impact: approximately -0.3 percentage points
-Peak lag: three quarters
-t-stat: -2.7

The effect was strongest in core inflation because persistent labor, services and input costs are harder for companies to absorb.

Long rates told a different story.

Changes in the 10-year yield, 30-year yield and real 10-year yield had no statistically meaningful relationship with future FCF margins.

The damage came from inflation compressing operating margins, not higher discount rates directly reducing cash generation.

The market’s timing is even more interesting.

Stocks did not anticipate the inflation surge.

They rallied during the year before core inflation accelerated.

Once inflation became visible, equities began selling off.

The FCF damage appeared two to four quarters later and was reported another six weeks after each quarter ended.

In other words, prices led the financial statements by roughly one quarter.

That is what happened in 2022.

The market sold the coming cash-flow deterioration before it appeared in reported results.

Could that be happening again?

Possibly.

The current decline may be pricing weaker 2027 cash generation caused by persistent inflation, tariffs and higher operating costs.

But there is a major caveat.

Nearly the entire historical relationship came from the 2021 through 2023 inflation shock.

Remove that period and almost nothing survives.

Core CPI’s two-quarter effect falls from a t-stat of -4.4 to -1.0.

Headline inflation and short rates even reverse direction.

This is not a universal market law.

It is one powerful episode.

That gives us a simple test for the current selloff:

Watch core inflation and FCF estimates, not just the 10-year yield.

If core inflation remains elevated and analysts begin cutting 2027 FCF margins, the market may be correctly front-running another cash-flow squeeze.

If inflation cools while FCF estimates remain intact, the market is fighting the last war.

Everyone is watching price.

The answer may arrive in the cash-flow revisions.

China kept exporting more but stopped importing USTs in 2014, and then dishoarded every year since.

Whenever someone points out that Russia's economy is smaller than Italy's, countless Russian bots and useful idiots reply that in purchasing power terms terms it's very different and Russia is really strong. No, it isn't. Russia is a paper tiger in both nominal GDP and PPP terms. Just look at the chart below, even in PPP terms, Russia is a clear outlier, two in five Russians lack decent sanitation. 

The reason is simple, Russia is a deeply corrupt state with one of the highest wealth concentrations in the world. Putin's cronies are billionaires who loot the country by transferring hundreds of billions into offshore accounts, while many ordinary Russians must go outside in winter, lack decent healthcare, and live in deep poverty, resulting in a life expectancy eight years lower than in Europe. Or should life expectancy also be adjusted for PPP?

There is no innovation, future technologies, or decent infrastructure. Young talent emigrates en masse, and the economy is held together by weapons production fired up on neighboring countries. That's not GDP creation, it's a desperate attempt to keep a house of cards together.

quoted.text:
There are two highly entertaining popular narratives about Russia:

1. “Russia is an economic power.” No, it’s not. Its economy is smaller than Italy’s despite vast natural resources. Russia has one of the world’s highest inequality rates, resource income is funneled by a small oligarch clique into offshore accounts, while two in five Russians lack a decent toilet. Purchasing power parity comparisons make little sense here. PPP works to compare similar countries like Spain and Poland, not a poor one like Russia versus a wealthy one like Italy. Russians pay less for bread because they are poor, not rich.

2. “Russia has much lower debt/GDP.” So what? It lacks a functioning mature financial system, foreigners avoid Russian bonds, and as a result Russia has a higher interest payment burden than highly indebted Southern European countries.
